source_text: Καὶ μὴν κἀκεῖνο πάντων παραλογώτατον, τὸ τοὺς μὲν θεσπισθέντας νόμους ἐπ᾿ ἀνθρώπους φέρειν, τῶν δὲ νομίμως ἢ παρανόμως πεπραγμένων τὴν δίκην ἐπὶ μόνας τρέπειν τὰς ψυχάς. Εἰ γὰρ ὁ τοὺς νόμους δεξάμενος οὗτος δέξαιτ᾿ ἂν δικαίως καὶ τῆς παρανομίας τὴν δίκην, ἐδέξατο δὲ τοὺς νόμους ἄνθρωπος, οὐ ψυχὴ καθ᾿ ἑαυτήν, ἄνθρωπον δεῖ καὶ τὴν ὑπὲρ τῶν ἡμαρτημένων ὑποσχεῖν δίκην, οὐ ψυχὴν καθ᾿ ἑαυτήν· ἐπεὶ μὴ ψυχαῖς ἐθέσπισε θεὸς ἀπέχεσθαι τῶν οὐδὲν αὐταῖς προσηκόντων, οἷον μοιχείας φόνου κλοπῆς ἁρπαγῆς τῆς κατὰ τῶν γεννησάντων ἀτιμίας, πάσης τε κοινῶς τῆς ἐπ᾿ ἀδικίᾳ καὶ βλάβῃ τῶν πέλας γινομένης ἐπιθυμίας. Οὔτε γὰρ τὸ Τίμα τὸν πατέρα σου καὶ τὴν μητέρα σου ψυχαῖς μόνον εὐάρμοστον, οὐ προσηκόντων αὐταῖς τῶν τοιούτων ὀνομάτων· οὐ γὰρ ψυχαὶ ψυχὰς γεννῶσαι τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς ἢ τῆς μητέρος οἰκειοῦνται προσηγορίαν, ἀλλ᾿ ἀνθρώπους ἄνθρωποι· οὔτε οὖν τὸ Οὐ μοιχεύσεις ἐπὶ ψυχῶν λεχθείῃ ποτ᾿ ἂν ἢ νοηθείη δεόντως, οὐκ οὔσης ἐν αὐταῖς τῆς κατὰ τὸ ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ διαφορᾶς οὐδὲ πρὸς μῖξίν τινος ἐπιτηδειότητος ἢ πρὸς ταύτην ὀρέξεως. Ὀρέξεως δὲ τοιαύτης οὐκ οὔσης, οὐδὲ μῖξιν εἶναι δυνατόν· παρ᾿ οἷς δὲ μῖξις οὐκ ἔστιν ὅλως, οὐδὲ ἔνθεσμος μῖξις, ὅπερ ἐστὶν ὁ γάμος· ἐννόμου δὲ μίξεως οὐκ οὔσης, οὐδὲ τὴν παράνομον καὶ τὴν ἐπ᾿ ἀλλοτρίᾳ γυναικὶ γινομένην ὄρεξιν ἢ μῖξιν εἶναι δυνατόν, τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι μοιχεία. Ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ τὸ κλοπὴν ἀπαγορεύειν ἢ τὴν τοῦ πλείονος ἐπιθυμίαν ψυχαῖς προσφυές· οὐδὲ γὰρ δέονται τούτων, ὧν οἱ δεόμενοι διὰ τὴν φυσικὴν ἔνδειαν ἢ χρείαν κλέπτειν εἰώθασιν ἢ λῃστεύειν, οἷον χρυσὸν ἢ ἄργυρον ἢ ζῶον ἢ ἄλλο τι τῶν πρὸς τροφὴν ἢ σκέπην ἢ χρῆσιν ἐπιτηδείων· ἀχρεῖον γὰρ ἀθανάτῳ φύσει πᾶν ὁπόσον τοῖς ἐνδεέσιν ὀρεκτὸν ὡς χρήσιμον. Ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μὲν ἐντελέστερος περὶ τούτων λόγος ἀφείσθω τοῖς σπουδαιότερον ἕκαστον σκοπεῖν βουλομένοις ἢ φιλοτιμότερον διαγωνίζεσθαι πρὸς τοὺς διαφερομένους. Ἡμῖν δὲ ἀρκούντων τῶν ἀρτίως εἰρημένων καὶ τῶν συμφώνως τούτοις τὴν ἀνάστασιν πιστουμένων, τὸ τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἐπὶ πλεῖον ἐνδιατρίβειν οὐκ ἔτ᾿ ἂν ἔχοι καιρόν· οὐ γὰρ τὸ μηδὲν παραλιπεῖν τῶν ἐνόντων εἰπεῖν πεποιήμεθα σκοπόν, ἀλλὰ τὸ κεφαλαιωδῶς ὑποδεῖξαι τοῖς συνελθοῦσιν ἅ χρὴ περὶ ἀναστάσεως φρονεῖν, καὶ τῇ δυνάμει τῶν παρόντων συμμετρῆσαι τὰς ἐπὶ τοῦτο φερούσας ἀφορμάς.
thought_title: Laws bind humans, so judgment must fall on humans, not souls alone
orientation: Athenagoras is arguing that divine justice requires the whole human being, not the soul alone, to be judged, and now presses the point that the commandments were given to humans, not to souls by themselves.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed that too is the most unreasonable of all, that they bring the laws that were ordained upon humans, but they turn the penalty of things done lawfully or unlawfully upon souls alone. For if the one who received the laws would justly receive also the penalty of the lawlessness, and a human received the laws, not a soul by itself, then a human must also undergo the penalty for the sins, not a soul by itself; since God did not ordain for souls to abstain from things that in no way pertain to them, such as adultery, murder, theft, robbery, dishonor against one's parents, and in general every desire that comes about for injustice and harm of neighbors. For neither is the 'Honor your father and your mother' fitting for souls alone, since such names do not pertain to them; for souls do not beget souls and so do not claim the title of father or mother, but humans beget humans; nor then would the 'You shall not commit adultery' ever be said or rightly understood of souls, since in them there is no difference according to male and female, nor any fitness for intercourse with anyone, nor desire for this. And when there is no such desire, intercourse is not possible either; and among those for whom there is no intercourse at all, there is no lawful intercourse, which is marriage; and when there is no lawful intercourse, neither the unlawful desire nor the intercourse that happens with another man's wife is possible, for this is adultery. But neither is forbidding theft or the desire for more natural to souls; for they do not need those things which those who need them because of natural lack or need are accustomed to steal or rob, such as gold or silver or an animal or anything else of the things suitable for food or shelter or use; for everything that is desired by the needy as useful is useless to an immortal nature. But let the more complete argument about these things be left to those who wish to examine each point more diligently or to contend more ambitiously against those who disagree. And since the things just said are sufficient for us, and the things that in agreement with them confirm the resurrection, to spend more time on the same points would no longer have occasion; for we have not made it our aim to leave out nothing of what is possible to say, but to show in summary form to those who have come together what one must think about the resurrection, and to measure by the power of what is present the starting points that lead to this.

choices.why: The superlative marks this as the height of the critics' inconsistency; 'unreasonable' captures the sense of going against sound reasoning.
In this judicial context δίκη is the punishment or retribution exacted for deeds, not the abstract concept of justice.
The idiom means to submit to or pay the penalty; 'undergo' preserves the passive subjection of the human being to punishment.
The phrase καθ᾿ ἑαυτήν stresses the soul considered in isolation from the body, which is the whole point of the argument.
In rhetorical usage ἀφορμή denotes the resources or grounds from which an argument proceeds; 'starting points' fits the summary purpose stated here.

bible_refs.note: Τίμα τὸν πατέρα σου καὶ τὴν μητέρα σου

pass_b_english: And indeed the most unreasonable thing of all is this: they bring the laws decreed for human beings, yet they turn the penalty for things done lawfully or unlawfully upon souls alone. For if the one who received the laws would also justly accept the penalty for lawbreaking, and it was a human being who received the laws, not a soul by itself, then a human being must undergo the penalty for sins, not a soul by itself. God did not decree to souls that they abstain from things that in no way pertain to them: adultery, murder, theft, robbery, dishonor toward parents, and in general every desire that leads to injustice and harm of neighbors.

For the command, "Honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12), is not fitting for souls alone, since such names do not pertain to them. Souls do not beget souls and so claim the title of father or mother; rather, human beings beget human beings. Nor would "You shall not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:14) ever be rightly spoken or understood of souls, since in them there is no distinction of male and female, no fitness for intercourse with anyone, and no desire for it. Where there is no such desire, intercourse cannot occur. And where there is no intercourse at all, there is no lawful intercourse, which is what marriage is. Where there is no lawful intercourse, there can be no unlawful desire or intercourse with another man's wife, and that is adultery.

Nor is the prohibition of theft or of greed for what belongs to another fitting for souls. They do not need the things that those who are in want are accustomed to steal or plunder because of natural lack or need: gold, silver, an animal, or anything else suited for food, shelter, or use. For everything that the needy desire as useful is useless to an immortal nature.

But let the more complete argument about these matters be left to those who wish to examine each point more carefully or to contend more vigorously against opponents. Since what has just been said is sufficient for us, along with what agrees with it in confirming the resurrection, there is no longer any occasion to dwell on these things at greater length. For our aim has not been to omit nothing that could be said, but to show in summary form to those assembled what they ought to think about the resurrection, and to measure the starting points that lead to it by the force of what is present.

problems.why: Exodus 20:14 is 'You shall not steal.' The adultery command is Exodus 20:13 (LXX 20:13/Heb 20:14).
problems.ruling: Claim is correct: Exodus 20:14 is 'You shall not steal' (οὐ κλέψεις); 'You shall not commit adultery' (οὐ μοιχεύσεις) is Exodus 20:13 in LXX, Hebrew 20:14.

problems.quote: they bring the laws that God has decreed against human beings
problems.source_quote: τὸ τοὺς μὲν θεσπισθέντας νόμους ἐπ᾿ ἀνθρώπους φέρειν
problems.why: "Against" reverses meaning: ἐπί here means "upon" or "to" (laws given TO humans), not against.
problems.fix: they bring the laws decreed for human beings

problems.quote: what has been done lawfully or unlawfully
problems.source_quote: τῶν δὲ νομίμως ἢ παρανόμως πεπραγμένων
problems.why: "Lawfully or unlawfully" misreads: νομίμως means "in accordance with law" but context demands "lawfully or contrary to law" as opposites; πεπραγμένων = things done, not "has been done."

problems.quote: the one who received the laws would justly undergo the penalty
problems.source_quote: ὁ τοὺς νόμους δεξάμενος οὗτος δέξαιτ᾿ ἂν δικαίως καὶ τῆς παρανομίας τὴν δίκην
problems.why: "Would justly undergo" is wrong: δέξαιτ᾿ ἂν δικαίως = "would justly accept/receive," not undergo; καὶ = "also," omitted in English.
problems.fix: the one who received the laws would also justly accept the penalty for lawbreaking

problems.why: "Desire for more" misses the specific sense: τοῦ πλείονος = "of what is more/more than enough," i.e., covetousness/greed for others' goods, not just "more."
problems.fix: desire for what belongs to another, or greed

last_rejected.source_quote: τῶν δὲ νομίμως ἢ παρανόμως πεπραγμένων
last_rejected.why: 'Lawfully or unlawfully' misreads: context requires 'in accordance with or against the laws', i.e., obedience or transgression, not 'lawfully done'.
last_rejected.fix: things done in obedience or transgression of the laws
last_rejected.ruling: νομίμως ἢ παρανόμως naturally means 'lawfully or unlawfully'; rendering is within normal range, no meaning lost.

polish.changed: Clarified the logical flow by making the contrast between laws given to human beings and penalties applied to souls alone more direct, marked the Scripture quotations explicitly as quotations with their references, and broke the dense argument into shorter paragraphs where the thought turns from the general principle to specific commandments and then to the conclusion.
